extracted.intended_audience: students and academic writers (undergraduate/graduate) and researchers preparing reports, essays, and arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for planning, drafting, and revising academic and research writing (reports, essays, arguments), including use of evidence, citations, structure, and ethical considerations. Also touches on some creative-writing elements (characters, clauses) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgments and responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgments and responses; anticipating objections and questions; framing responses; predictable disagreements; selecting objections for response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing the body and responses, anticipate readers' objections and questions, select which objections to answer, frame responses clearly, and be aware of common predictable disagreements. See related guidance on imagining audience and framing rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor active-voice verbs to improve clarity and immediacy of prose (see style entries). Avoid excessive passive constructions that obscure agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments (making and structuring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments: anticipating objections and questions; background information; common mistakes; complex arguments; evidence for support; making a claim; reasons for support; revisions; subclaims; supporting a claim; thickening; warrants of relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build arguments by making explicit claims, supplying reasons and evidence, adding and organizing subclaims, anticipating objections, thickening lines of support where necessary, and ensuring each claim has a clear warrant of relevance. Watch for common argumentative mistakes; plan complex arguments with clear structure and revisions in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience (imagining and responding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience: anticipating objections and questions; imagining your audience; responses to audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly imagine the reader to shape tone, level of detail, and which objections to address. Tailor explanations and evidence to the audience's knowledge and concerns; use 'elevator stories' and concise openings where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations and citation styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations: author-date styles (APA), author-title styles, parenthetical citations, endnotes, footnotes; Chicago and APA styles referenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the citation style appropriate to discipline (APA, Chicago, etc.), be consistent, provide full bibliographic data, and guard against plagiarism by citing all borrowed ideas and quotations. See entries for specific style manuals (Chicago Manual of Style, APA, Bluebook for legal citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of a report: structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Body of a report: acknowledgments and responses; defining terms; key concepts; ordering of information; planning a draft; presenting evidence; revising; sections and subsections; warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the report body around clear sections and subsections, define key terms early, present evidence in a planned order that clarifies relevance, and use warrants to link evidence to claims. Plan the draft structure before detailed writing and revise sections for coherence and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charts, tables, and graphs (figures and graphic displays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts and graphs: bar charts, area charts, histograms, bubble charts, image charts, figures, drawings; guidance on ethical considerations for graphic displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the chart type appropriate for the data (e.g., bar charts, histograms). Create clear, honest graphic displays that avoid misleading scaling or omission of relevant data. Follow ethical guidance for visual presentation and captions; label axes and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: formulation and qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims: being explicit; being significant; being specific; evaluating a claim; hedges; limiting conditions; main claims; opposite claims; qualifying a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make claims explicit and specific, state their significance, qualify them with limiting conditions and hedges where appropriate, consider and address opposing claims, and evaluate claims against available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity. See style (includes active verbs, plain prose, avoiding cognitive overload).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear prose: use straightforward sentence structure, active verbs, define technical terms, avoid unnecessary jargon, and present information to minimize cognitive overload. Use style manuals for discipline-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting (planning, quotations, paraphrasing, and anti-plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting: planning for, drafting, citations, guarding against plagiarism, headings and subheadings, paraphrasing, quotations, summarizing, using key concepts, writer's block, revising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan drafts with an outline, use headings and subheadings for structure, quote sparingly and cite source pages, paraphrase correctly and cite, summarize secondary sources, and employ revision cycles. Use strategies to overcome writer's block and always check attribution to avoid plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions: calling for more research; closing sentences; drafting; formulation of claims; revising; stating significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude by restating main claims, explaining their significance, suggesting directions for further research if appropriate, and using effective closing sentences. Revise conclusions to ensure they follow logically from evidence presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations (honesty, copyrights, human subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical considerations: copyrights; for graphic displays; human subjects; intellectual honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to ethical norms: respect copyrights, properly anonymize or obtain consent for human-subject data, present graphic displays honestly, and maintain intellectual honesty in claims, citations, and reporting of methods and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence (evaluation and sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence: kinds of evidence; evaluating evidence; foundational metaphors for evidence; precise statements of evidence; reliability of evidence; sufficiency of evidence; reports of evidence; supporting a claim; types of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence for reliability, relevance, and sufficiency. Make precise statements about what evidence shows, triangulate across source types when possible, and ensure evidence is explicitly tied to claims via warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagining the reader (reader-awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagining the reader: imagine your audience; anticipate objections; shape responses and level of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reader-awareness to decide tone, where to provide background, which objections to preempt, and how technical the language should be. Techniques include writing elevator stories and outlining reader questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of information and sectioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordering of information; sections and subsections; headings and subheadings; order of information in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence information so that definitions and key concepts come early, evidence builds toward claims, and sections flow logically. Use descriptive headings to guide readers and signal transitions between ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bibliographic resources and databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliographies, bibliographic data, databases, indexes (ERIC, PsycINFO, ISI Web of Science, etc.), encyclopedias, finding topics, specialized indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate and use appropriate authoritative sources for discipline (databases, encyclopedias, indexes). Record full bibliographic data for citations and ensure literature searches are systematic and appropriate for the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Guarding against plagiarism; citations; paraphrasing; summarizing; quoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute ideas and direct quotations. Paraphrase genuinely (not merely change a few words) and cite the source. Keep careful notes of sources while drafting to avoid accidental plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (for fiction/creative writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters (252-60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters fully: attend to clauses, actions, motivations, contradictions, and development. (Index indicates a dedicated section on character construction and related grammatical matters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning a project; choosing and focusing a topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a project; choosing a topic; finding a topic; focusing your topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin projects by selecting a manageable topic, focus it to fit scope and audience, and use early planning steps to outline claims and evidence. Use bibliographic searches and exploratory writing to refine focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revising and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Revising: draft revision cycles, specific revision items (arguments, clarity, evidence, organization), and editing mechanics (citations, style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise for argument strength, clarity, evidence sufficiency, and logical organization. Edit in passes: high-level structure first, then paragraph/sentence clarity, then citation/formatting and copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrants of relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants of relevance: ensure evidence is linked to claims through explicit warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State or make clear the relevance of evidence to claims so readers see why a piece of evidence supports the argument. Explicit warrants reduce hidden assumptions and improve persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures, drawings and other non-textual materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, drawings, images, captions and labeling; guidance on presenting non-textual materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate figures and drawings where they clarify data or concepts; include descriptive captions, cite sources for images, and ensure visuals are referenced and explained in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and discipline-specific manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Style manuals and guides cited: Chicago Manual of Style, APA Publication Manual, CSE manual, AIP Style Manual, ACS Style Guide, Bluebook (legal citation), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the appropriate style manual for formatting, citation, and discipline-specific conventions. Use the manual consistently throughout the manuscript.
